display_name: Pulmonary Embolism with Right Heart Strain
overview: Pulmonary embolism is a potentially life-threatening condition in which a blood clot blocks one or more pulmonary arteries in the lungs. Most pulmonary emboli originate from deep vein thrombosis in the legs and travel through the venous circulation to the lungs. Large or multiple emboli can significantly increase pulmonary vascular resistance, causing acute right ventricular pressure overload, right ventricular dilation, right ventricular strain, reduced cardiac output, shock, and death. Right ventricular strain on ECG may provide evidence of acute hemodynamic stress but cannot independently confirm pulmonary embolism.
ecg_clues: t wave inversion in lead iii
ecg_limitations: ecg alone cannot diagnose pulmonary embolism
many patients with pulmonary embolism have nonspecific ecg findings
absence of right ventricular strain does not exclude pulmonary embolism
ecg cannot determine pulmonary artery obstruction severity
ecg findings may overlap with pulmonary hypertension and chronic lung disease
causes: blood clot migration from lower extremities

history_questions: Did the shortness of breath start suddenly?
Do you have chest pain when breathing deeply?
Do you have swelling in one leg?
Have you recently been immobilized or bedridden?
Have you recently taken a long flight or car trip?
Do you have a history of deep vein thrombosis?
Have you had a pulmonary embolism before?
Are you pregnant or recently postpartum?

when_to_seek_help: rapid heart rate with breathing difficulty

followup_questions.sudden_dyspnea: Did the shortness of breath start suddenly?
followup_questions.pleuritic_chest_pain: Does the chest pain worsen when taking a deep breath?
followup_questions.syncope: Have you fainted or nearly fainted recently?
followup_questions.leg_swelling: Do you have swelling in one leg?
followup_questions.leg_pain: Do you have calf pain or tenderness?
followup_questions.history_of_dvt: Have you ever been diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis?
followup_questions.history_of_pe: Have you had a pulmonary embolism before?
followup_questions.recent_surgery: Have you undergone surgery within the last month?
followup_questions.recent_immobilization: Have you recently been bedridden or unable to move normally?
followup_questions.active_cancer: Are you currently being treated for cancer?
followup_questions.pregnancy: Are you currently pregnant or recently postpartum?
followup_questions.oxygen_saturation: Have you been told that your oxygen level is low?

confidence_rules: pleuritic chest pain strongly increases suspicion
unilateral leg swelling strongly increases suspicion
history of dvt strongly increases suspicion
history of pulmonary embolism strongly increases suspicion
right ventricular strain ecg pattern increases suspicion
agent_reasoning_hints: ecg alone cannot diagnose pulmonary embolism
absence of right ventricular strain does not exclude pulmonary embolism
right ventricular strain pattern increases suspicion but is not specific
deep vein thrombosis symptoms significantly increase probability
sudden unexplained dyspnea should raise concern
ct pulmonary angiography is frequently required for confirmation
massive pulmonary embolism can cause acute right ventricular failure
pulmonary embolism is a medical emergency when associated with shock or syncope
source_notes: most pulmonary emboli originate from deep vein thrombosis
pulmonary embolism may be life threatening
right ventricular strain reflects increased right ventricular workload
massive pulmonary embolism may cause acute right ventricular dilation
pulmonary embolism can lead to pulmonary hypertension
ct pulmonary angiography is a common confirmatory test
ecg findings support suspicion but do not establish diagnosis
